author: François de La Rochefoucauld
translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
why: One-line truths on vanity; ideal swipe cards

rochefoucauld.1.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.1.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.1.text: What we term virtue is often but a mass of various actions and divers interests, which fortune, or our own industry, manage to arrange; and it is not always from valour or from chastity that men are brave, and women chaste.

rochefoucauld.2.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.2.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.2.text: Self-love is the greatest of flatterers.

rochefoucauld.3.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.3.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.3.text: Whatever discoveries have been made in the region of self-love, there remain many unexplored territories there.

rochefoucauld.4.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.4.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.4.text: Self love is more cunning than the most cunning man in the world.

rochefoucauld.5.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.5.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.5.text: The duration of our passions is no more dependant upon us than the duration of our life.

rochefoucauld.6.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.6.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.6.text: Passion often renders the most clever man a fool, and even sometimes renders the most foolish man clever.

rochefoucauld.7.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.7.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.7.text: Great and striking actions which dazzle the eyes are represented by politicians as the effect of great designs, instead of which they are commonly caused by the temper and the passions. Thus the war between Augustus and Anthony, which is set down to the ambition they entertained of making themselves masters of the world, was probably but an effect of jealousy.

rochefoucauld.8.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.8.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.8.text: The passions are the only advocates which always persuade. They are a natural art, the rules of which are infallible; and the simplest man with passion will be more persuasive than the most eloquent without.

rochefoucauld.9.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.9.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.9.text: The passions possess a certain injustice and self interest which makes it dangerous to follow them, and in reality we should distrust them even when they appear most trustworthy.

rochefoucauld.10.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.10.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.10.text: In the human heart there is a perpetual generation of passions; so that the ruin of one is almost always the foundation of another.

rochefoucauld.11.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.11.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.11.text: Passions often produce their contraries: avarice sometimes leads to prodigality, and prodigality to avarice; we are often obstinate through weakness and daring though timidity.

rochefoucauld.12.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.12.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.12.text: Whatever care we take to conceal our passions under the appearances of piety and honour, they are always to be seen through these veils.

rochefoucauld.13.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.13.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.13.text: Our self love endures more impatiently the condemnation of our tastes than of our opinions.

rochefoucauld.14.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.14.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.14.text: Men are not only prone to forget benefits and injuries; they even hate those who have obliged them, and cease to hate those who have injured them. The necessity of revenging an injury or of recompensing a benefit seems a slavery to which they are unwilling to submit.

rochefoucauld.15.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.15.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.15.text: The clemency of Princes is often but policy to win the affections of the people.

rochefoucauld.16.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.16.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.16.text: This clemency of which they make a merit, arises oftentimes from vanity, sometimes from idleness, oftentimes from fear, and almost always from all three combined.

rochefoucauld.17.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.17.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.17.text: The moderation of those who are happy arises from the calm which good fortune bestows upon their temper.

rochefoucauld.18.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.18.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.18.text: Moderation is caused by the fear of exciting the envy and contempt which those merit who are intoxicated with their good fortune; it is a vain display of our strength of mind, and in short the moderation of men at their greatest height is only a desire to appear greater than their fortune.

rochefoucauld.19.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.19.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.19.text: We have all sufficient strength to support the misfortunes of others.

rochefoucauld.20.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.20.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.20.text: The constancy of the wise is only the talent of concealing the agitation of their hearts.

rochefoucauld.21.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.21.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.21.text: Those who are condemned to death affect sometimes a constancy and contempt for death which is only the fear of facing it; so that one may say that this constancy and contempt are to their mind what the bandage is to their eyes.

rochefoucauld.22.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.22.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.22.text: Philosophy triumphs easily over past evils and future evils; but present evils triumph over it.

rochefoucauld.23.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.23.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.23.text: Few people know death, we only endure it, usually from determination, and even from stupidity and custom; and most men only die because they know not how to prevent dying.

rochefoucauld.24.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.24.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.24.text: When great men permit themselves to be cast down by the continuance of misfortune, they show us that they were only sustained by ambition, and not by their mind; so that PLUS a great vanity, heroes are made like other men.

rochefoucauld.25.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.25.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.25.text: We need greater virtues to sustain good than evil fortune.

rochefoucauld.26.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.26.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.26.text: Neither the sun nor death can be looked at without winking.

rochefoucauld.27.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.27.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.27.text: People are often vain of their passions, even of the worst, but envy is a passion so timid and shame-faced that no one ever dare avow her.

rochefoucauld.28.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.28.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.28.text: Jealousy is in a manner just and reasonable, as it tends to preserve a good which belongs, or which we believe belongs to us, on the other hand envy is a fury which cannot endure the happiness of others.

rochefoucauld.29.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.29.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.29.text: The evil that we do does not attract to us so much persecution and hatred as our good qualities.

rochefoucauld.30.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.30.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.30.text: We have more strength than will; and it is often merely for an excuse we say things are impossible.

rochefoucauld.31.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.31.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.31.text: If we had no faults we should not take so much pleasure in noting those of others.

rochefoucauld.32.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.32.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.32.text: Jealousy lives upon doubt; and comes to an end or becomes a fury as soon as it passes from doubt to certainty.

rochefoucauld.33.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.33.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.33.text: Pride indemnifies itself and loses nothing even when it casts away vanity.

rochefoucauld.34.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.34.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.34.text: If we had no pride we should not complain of that of others.

rochefoucauld.35.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.35.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.35.text: Pride is much the same in all men, the only difference is the method and manner of showing it.

rochefoucauld.36.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.36.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.36.text: It would seem that nature, which has so wisely ordered the organs of our body for our happiness, has also given us pride to spare us the mortification of knowing our imperfections.

rochefoucauld.37.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.37.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.37.text: Pride has a larger part than goodness in our remonstrances with those who commit faults, and we reprove them not so much to correct as to persuade them that we ourselves are free from faults.

rochefoucauld.38.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.38.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.38.text: We promise according to our hopes; we perform according to our fears.

rochefoucauld.39.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.39.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.39.text: Interest speaks all sorts of tongues and plays all sorts of characters; even that of disinterestedness.

rochefoucauld.40.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.40.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.40.text: Interest blinds some and makes some see.

rochefoucauld.41.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.41.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.41.text: Those who apply themselves too closely to little things often become incapable of great things.

rochefoucauld.42.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.42.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.42.text: We have not enough strength to follow all our reason.

rochefoucauld.43.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.43.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.43.text: A man often believes himself leader when he is led; as his mind endeavours to reach one goal, his heart insensibly drags him towards another.

rochefoucauld.44.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.44.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.44.text: Strength and weakness of mind are mis-named; they are really only the good or happy arrangement of our bodily organs.

rochefoucauld.45.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.45.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.45.text: The caprice of our temper is even more whimsical than that of Fortune.

rochefoucauld.46.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.46.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.46.text: The attachment or indifference which philosophers have shown to life is only the style of their self love, about which we can no more dispute than of that of the palate or of the choice of colours.

rochefoucauld.47.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.47.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.47.text: Our temper sets a price upon every gift that we receive from fortune.

rochefoucauld.48.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.48.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.48.text: Happiness is in the taste, and not in the things themselves; we are happy from possessing what we like, not from possessing what others like.

rochefoucauld.49.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.49.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.49.text: We are never so happy or so unhappy as we suppose.

rochefoucauld.50.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.50.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.50.text: Those who think they have merit persuade themselves that they are honoured by being unhappy, in order to persuade others and themselves that they are worthy to be the butt of fortune.

rochefoucauld.51.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.51.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.51.text: Nothing should so much diminish the satisfaction which we feel with ourselves as seeing that we disapprove at one time of that which we approve of at another.

rochefoucauld.52.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.52.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.52.text: Whatever difference there appears in our fortunes, there is nevertheless a certain compensation of good and evil which renders them equal.

rochefoucauld.53.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.53.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.53.text: Whatever great advantages nature may give, it is not she alone, but fortune also that makes the hero.

rochefoucauld.54.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.54.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.54.text: The contempt of riches in philosophers was only a hidden desire to avenge their merit upon the injustice of fortune, by despising the very goods of which fortune had deprived them; it was a secret to guard themselves against the degradation of poverty, it was a back way by which to arrive at that distinction which they could not gain by riches.

rochefoucauld.55.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.55.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.55.text: The hate of favourites is only a love of favour. The envy of NOT possessing it, consoles and softens its regrets by the contempt it evinces for those who possess it, and we refuse them our homage, not being able to detract from them what attracts that of the rest of the world.

rochefoucauld.56.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.56.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.56.text: To establish ourselves in the world we do everything to appear as if we were established.

rochefoucauld.57.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.57.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.57.text: Although men flatter themselves with their great actions, they are not so often the result of a great design as of chance.

rochefoucauld.58.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.58.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.58.text: It would seem that our actions have lucky or unlucky stars to which they owe a great part of the blame or praise which is given them.

rochefoucauld.59.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.59.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.59.text: There are no accidents so unfortunate from which skilful men will not draw some advantage, nor so fortunate that foolish men will not turn them to their hurt.

rochefoucauld.60.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.60.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.60.text: Fortune turns all things to the advantage of those on whom she smiles.

rochefoucauld.61.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.61.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.61.text: The happiness or unhappiness of men depends no less upon their dispositions than their fortunes.

rochefoucauld.62.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.62.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.62.text: Sincerity is an openness of heart; we find it in very few people; what we usually see is only an artful dissimulation to win the confidence of others.

rochefoucauld.63.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.63.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.63.text: The aversion to lying is often a hidden ambition to render our words credible and weighty, and to attach a religious aspect to our conversation.

rochefoucauld.64.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.64.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.64.text: Truth does not do as much good in the world, as its counterfeits do evil.

rochefoucauld.65.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.65.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.65.text: There is no praise we have not lavished upon Prudence; and yet she cannot assure to us the most trifling event.

rochefoucauld.66.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.66.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.66.text: A clever man ought to so regulate his interests that each will fall in due order. Our greediness so often troubles us, making us run after so many things at the same time, that while we too eagerly look after the least we miss the greatest.

rochefoucauld.67.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.67.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.67.text: What grace is to the body good sense is to the mind.

rochefoucauld.68.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.68.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.68.text: It is difficult to define love; all we can say is, that in the soul it is a desire to rule, in the mind it is a sympathy, and in the body it is a hidden and delicate wish to possess what we love—Plus many mysteries.

rochefoucauld.69.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.69.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.69.text: If there is a pure love, exempt from the mixture of our other passions, it is that which is concealed at the bottom of the heart and of which even ourselves are ignorant.

rochefoucauld.70.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.70.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.70.text: There is no disguise which can long hide love where it exists, nor feign it where it does not.

rochefoucauld.71.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.71.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.71.text: There are few people who would not be ashamed of being beloved when they love no longer.

rochefoucauld.72.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.72.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.72.text: If we judge of love by the majority of its results it rather resembles hatred than friendship.

rochefoucauld.73.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.73.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.73.text: We may find women who have never indulged in an intrigue, but it is rare to find those who have intrigued but once.

rochefoucauld.74.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.74.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.74.text: There is only one sort of love, but there are a thousand different copies.

rochefoucauld.75.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.75.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.75.text: Neither love nor fire can subsist without perpetual motion; both cease to live so soon as they cease to hope, or to fear.

rochefoucauld.76.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.76.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.76.text: There is real love just as there are real ghosts; every person speaks of it, few persons have seen it.

rochefoucauld.77.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.77.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.77.text: Love lends its name to an infinite number of engagements (Commerces) which are attributed to it, but with which it has no more concern than the Doge has with all that is done in Venice.

rochefoucauld.78.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.78.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.78.text: The love of justice is simply in the majority of men the fear of suffering injustice.

rochefoucauld.79.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.79.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.79.text: Silence is the best resolve for him who distrusts himself.

rochefoucauld.80.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.80.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.80.text: What renders us so changeable in our friendship is, that it is difficult to know the qualities of the soul, but easy to know those of the mind.

rochefoucauld.81.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.81.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.81.text: We can love nothing but what agrees with us, and we can only follow our taste or our pleasure when we prefer our friends to ourselves; nevertheless it is only by that preference that friendship can be true and perfect.

rochefoucauld.82.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.82.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.82.text: Reconciliation with our enemies is but a desire to better our condition, a weariness of war, the fear of some unlucky accident.

rochefoucauld.83.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.83.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.83.text: What men term friendship is merely a partnership with a collection of reciprocal interests, and an exchange of favours—in fact it is but a trade in which self love always expects to gain something.

rochefoucauld.84.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.84.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.84.text: It is more disgraceful to distrust than to be deceived by our friends.

rochefoucauld.85.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.85.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.85.text: We often persuade ourselves to love people who are more powerful than we are, yet interest alone produces our friendship; we do not give our hearts away for the good we wish to do, but for that we expect to receive.

rochefoucauld.86.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.86.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.86.text: Our distrust of another justifies his deceit.

rochefoucauld.87.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.87.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.87.text: Men would not live long in society were they not the dupes of each other.

rochefoucauld.88.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.88.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.88.text: Self love increases or diminishes for us the good qualities of our friends, in proportion to the satisfaction we feel with them, and we judge of their merit by the manner in which they act towards us.

rochefoucauld.89.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.89.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.89.text: Everyone blames his memory, no one blames his judgment.

rochefoucauld.90.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.90.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.90.text: In the intercourse of life, we please more by our faults than by our good qualities.

rochefoucauld.91.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.91.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.91.text: The largest ambition has the least appearance of ambition when it meets with an absolute impossibility in compassing its object.

rochefoucauld.92.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.92.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.92.text: To awaken a man who is deceived as to his own merit is to do him as bad a turn as that done to the Athenian madman who was happy in believing that all the ships touching at the port belonged to him.

rochefoucauld.93.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.93.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.93.text: Old men delight in giving good advice as a consolation for the fact that they can no longer set bad examples.

rochefoucauld.94.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.94.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.94.text: Great names degrade instead of elevating those who know not how to sustain them.

rochefoucauld.95.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.95.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.95.text: The test of extraordinary merit is to see those who envy it the most yet obliged to praise it.

rochefoucauld.96.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.96.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.96.text: A man is perhaps ungrateful, but often less chargeable with ingratitude than his benefactor is.

rochefoucauld.97.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.97.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.97.text: We are deceived if we think that mind and judgment are two different matters: judgment is but the extent of the light of the mind. This light penetrates to the bottom of matters; it remarks all that can be remarked, and perceives what appears imperceptible. Therefore we must agree that it is the extent of the light in the mind that produces all the effects which we attribute to judgment.

rochefoucauld.98.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.98.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.98.text: Everyone praises his heart, none dare praise their understanding.

rochefoucauld.99.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.99.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.99.text: Politeness of mind consists in thinking chaste and refined thoughts.

rochefoucauld.100.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.100.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.100.text: Gallantry of mind is saying the most empty things in an agreeable manner.

rochefoucauld.101.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.101.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.101.text: Ideas often flash across our minds more complete than we could make them after much labour.

rochefoucauld.102.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.102.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.102.text: The head is ever the dupe of the heart.

rochefoucauld.103.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.103.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.103.text: Those who know their minds do not necessarily know their hearts.

rochefoucauld.104.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.104.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.104.text: Men and things have each their proper perspective; to judge rightly of some it is necessary to see them near, of others we can never judge rightly but at a distance.

rochefoucauld.105.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.105.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.105.text: A man for whom accident discovers sense, is not a rational being. A man only is so who understands, who distinguishes, who tests it.

rochefoucauld.106.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.106.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.106.text: To understand matters rightly we should understand their details, and as that knowledge is almost infinite, our knowledge is always superficial and imperfect.

rochefoucauld.107.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.107.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.107.text: One kind of flirtation is to boast we never flirt.

rochefoucauld.108.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.108.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.108.text: The head cannot long play the part of the heart.

rochefoucauld.109.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.109.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.109.text: Youth changes its tastes by the warmth of its blood, age retains its tastes by habit.

rochefoucauld.110.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.110.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.110.text: Nothing is given so profusely as advice.

rochefoucauld.111.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.111.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.111.text: The more we love a woman the more prone we are to hate her.

rochefoucauld.112.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.112.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.112.text: The blemishes of the mind, like those of the face, increase by age.

rochefoucauld.113.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.113.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.113.text: There may be good but there are no pleasant marriages.

rochefoucauld.114.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.114.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.114.text: We are inconsolable at being deceived by our enemies and betrayed by our friends, yet still we are often content to be thus served by ourselves.

rochefoucauld.115.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.115.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.115.text: It is as easy unwittingly to deceive oneself as to deceive others.

rochefoucauld.116.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.116.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.116.text: Nothing is less sincere than the way of asking and giving advice. The person asking seems to pay deference to the opinion of his friend, while thinking in reality of making his friend approve his opinion and be responsible for his conduct. The person giving the advice returns the confidence placed in him by eager and disinterested zeal, in doing which he is usually guided only by his own interest or reputation.

rochefoucauld.117.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.117.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.117.text: The most subtle of our acts is to simulate blindness for snares that we know are set for us. We are never so easily deceived as when trying to deceive.

rochefoucauld.118.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.118.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.118.text: The intention of never deceiving often exposes us to deception.

rochefoucauld.119.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.119.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.119.text: We become so accustomed to disguise ourselves to others that at last we are disguised to ourselves.

rochefoucauld.120.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.120.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.120.text: We often act treacherously more from weakness than from a fixed motive.

rochefoucauld.121.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.121.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.121.text: We frequently do good to enable us with impunity to do evil.

rochefoucauld.122.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.122.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.122.text: If we conquer our passions it is more from their weakness than from our strength.

rochefoucauld.123.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.123.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.123.text: If we never flattered ourselves we should have but scant pleasure.

rochefoucauld.124.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.124.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.124.text: The most deceitful persons spend their lives in blaming deceit, so as to use it on some great occasion to promote some great interest.

rochefoucauld.125.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.125.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.125.text: The daily employment of cunning marks a little mind, it generally happens that those who resort to it in one respect to protect themselves lay themselves open to attack in another.

rochefoucauld.126.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.126.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.126.text: Cunning and treachery are the offspring of incapacity.

rochefoucauld.127.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.127.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.127.text: The true way to be deceived is to think oneself more knowing than others.

rochefoucauld.128.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.128.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.128.text: Too great cleverness is but deceptive delicacy, true delicacy is the most substantial cleverness.

rochefoucauld.129.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.129.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.129.text: It is sometimes necessary to play the fool to avoid being deceived by cunning men.

rochefoucauld.130.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.130.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.130.text: Weakness is the only fault which cannot be cured.

rochefoucauld.131.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.131.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.131.text: The smallest fault of women who give themselves up to love is to love.

rochefoucauld.132.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.132.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.132.text: It is far easier to be wise for others than to be so for oneself.

rochefoucauld.133.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.133.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.133.text: The only good examples are those, that make us see the absurdity of bad originals.

rochefoucauld.134.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.134.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.134.text: We are never so ridiculous from the habits we have as from those that we affect to have.

rochefoucauld.135.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.135.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.135.text: We sometimes differ more widely from ourselves than we do from others.

rochefoucauld.136.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.136.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.136.text: There are some who never would have loved if they never had heard it spoken of.

rochefoucauld.137.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.137.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.137.text: When not prompted by vanity we say little.

rochefoucauld.138.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.138.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.138.text: A man would rather say evil of himself than say nothing.

rochefoucauld.139.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.139.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.139.text: One of the reasons that we find so few persons rational and agreeable in conversation is there is hardly a person who does not think more of what he wants to say than of his answer to what is said. The most clever and polite are content with only seeming attentive while we perceive in their mind and eyes that at the very time they are wandering from what is said and desire to return to what they want to say. Instead of considering that the worst way to persuade or please others is to try thus strongly to please ourselves, and that to listen well and to answer well are some of the greatest charms we can have in conversation.

rochefoucauld.140.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.140.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.140.text: If it was not for the company of fools, a witty man would often be greatly at a loss.

rochefoucauld.141.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.141.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.141.text: We often boast that we are never bored, but yet we are so conceited that we do not perceive how often we bore others.

rochefoucauld.142.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.142.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.142.text: As it is the mark of great minds to say many things in a few words, so it is that of little minds to use many words to say nothing.

rochefoucauld.143.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.143.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.143.text: It is oftener by the estimation of our own feelings that we exaggerate the good qualities of others than by their merit, and when we praise them we wish to attract their praise.

rochefoucauld.144.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.144.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.144.text: We do not like to praise, and we never praise without a motive. Praise is flattery, artful, hidden, delicate, which gratifies differently him who praises and him who is praised. The one takes it as the reward of merit, the other bestows it to show his impartiality and knowledge.

rochefoucauld.145.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.145.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.145.text: We often select envenomed praise which, by a reaction upon those we praise, shows faults we could not have shown by other means.

rochefoucauld.146.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.146.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.146.text: Usually we only praise to be praised.

rochefoucauld.147.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.147.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.147.text: Few are sufficiently wise to prefer censure which is useful to praise which is treacherous.

rochefoucauld.148.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.148.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.148.text: Some reproaches praise; some praises reproach.

rochefoucauld.149.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.149.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.149.text: The refusal of praise is only the wish to be praised twice.

rochefoucauld.150.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.150.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.150.text: The desire which urges us to deserve praise strengthens our good qualities, and praise given to wit, valour, and beauty, tends to increase them.

rochefoucauld.151.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.151.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.151.text: It is easier to govern others than to prevent being governed.

rochefoucauld.152.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.152.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.152.text: If we never flattered ourselves the flattery of others would not hurt us.

rochefoucauld.153.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.153.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.153.text: Nature makes merit but fortune sets it to work.

rochefoucauld.154.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.154.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.154.text: Fortune cures us of many faults that reason could not.

rochefoucauld.155.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.155.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.155.text: There are some persons who only disgust with their abilities, there are persons who please even with their faults.

rochefoucauld.156.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.156.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.156.text: There are persons whose only merit consists in saying and doing stupid things at the right time, and who ruin all if they change their manners.

rochefoucauld.157.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.157.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.157.text: The fame of great men ought always to be estimated by the means used to acquire it.

rochefoucauld.158.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.158.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.158.text: Flattery is base coin to which only our vanity gives currency.

rochefoucauld.159.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.159.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.159.text: It is not enough to have great qualities, we should also have the management of them.

rochefoucauld.160.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.160.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.160.text: However brilliant an action it should not be esteemed great unless the result of a great motive.

rochefoucauld.161.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.161.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.161.text: A certain harmony should be kept between actions and ideas if we desire to estimate the effects that they produce.

rochefoucauld.162.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.162.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.162.text: The art of using moderate abilities to advantage wins praise, and often acquires more reputation than real brilliancy.

rochefoucauld.163.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.163.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.163.text: Numberless arts appear foolish whose secret motives are most wise and weighty.

rochefoucauld.164.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.164.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.164.text: It is much easier to seem fitted for posts we do not fill than for those we do.

rochefoucauld.165.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.165.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.165.text: Ability wins us the esteem of the true men, luck that of the people.

rochefoucauld.166.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.166.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.166.text: The world oftener rewards the appearance of merit than merit itself.

rochefoucauld.167.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.167.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.167.text: Avarice is more opposed to economy than to liberality.

rochefoucauld.168.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.168.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.168.text: However deceitful hope may be, yet she carries us on pleasantly to the end of life.

rochefoucauld.169.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.169.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.169.text: Idleness and fear keeps us in the path of duty, but our virtue often gets the praise.

rochefoucauld.170.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.170.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.170.text: If one acts rightly and honestly, it is difficult to decide whether it is the effect of integrity or skill.

rochefoucauld.171.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.171.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.171.text: As rivers are lost in the sea so are virtues in self.

rochefoucauld.172.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.172.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.172.text: If we thoroughly consider the varied effects of indifference we find we miscarry more in our duties than in our interests.

rochefoucauld.173.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.173.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.173.text: There are different kinds of curiosity: one springs from interest, which makes us desire to know everything that may be profitable to us; another from pride, which springs from a desire of knowing what others are ignorant of.

rochefoucauld.174.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.174.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.174.text: It is far better to accustom our mind to bear the ills we have than to speculate on those which may befall us.

rochefoucauld.175.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.175.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.175.text: Constancy in love is a perpetual inconstancy which causes our heart to attach itself to all the qualities of the person we love in succession, sometimes giving the preference to one, sometimes to another. This constancy is merely inconstancy fixed, and limited to the same person.

rochefoucauld.176.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.176.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.176.text: There are two kinds of constancy in love, one arising from incessantly finding in the loved one fresh objects to love, the other from regarding it as a point of honour to be constant.

rochefoucauld.177.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.177.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.177.text: Perseverance is not deserving of blame or praise, as it is merely the continuance of tastes and feelings which we can neither create or destroy.

rochefoucauld.178.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.178.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.178.text: What makes us like new studies is not so much the weariness we have of the old or the wish for change as the desire to be admired by those who know more than ourselves, and the hope of advantage over those who know less.

rochefoucauld.179.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.179.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.179.text: We sometimes complain of the levity of our friends to justify our own by anticipation.

rochefoucauld.180.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.180.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.180.text: Our repentance is not so much sorrow for the ill we have done as fear of the ill that may happen to us.

rochefoucauld.181.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.181.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.181.text: One sort of inconstancy springs from levity or weakness of mind, and makes us accept everyone's opinion, and another more excusable comes from a surfeit of matter.

rochefoucauld.182.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.182.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.182.text: Vices enter into the composition of virtues as poison into that of medicines. Prudence collects and blends the two and renders them useful against the ills of life.

rochefoucauld.183.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.183.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.183.text: For the credit of virtue we must admit that the greatest misfortunes of men are those into which they fall through their crimes.

rochefoucauld.184.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.184.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.184.text: We admit our faults to repair by our sincerity the evil we have done in the opinion of others.

rochefoucauld.185.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.185.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.185.text: There are both heroes of evil and heroes of good.

rochefoucauld.186.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.186.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.186.text: We do not despise all who have vices, but we do despise all who have not virtues.

rochefoucauld.187.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.187.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.187.text: The name of virtue is as useful to our interest as that of vice.

rochefoucauld.188.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.188.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.188.text: The health of the mind is not less uncertain than that of the body, and when passions seem furthest removed we are no less in danger of infection than of falling ill when we are well.

rochefoucauld.189.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.189.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.189.text: It seems that nature has at man's birth fixed the bounds of his virtues and vices.

rochefoucauld.190.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.190.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.190.text: Great men should not have great faults.

rochefoucauld.191.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.191.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.191.text: We may say vices wait on us in the course of our life as the landlords with whom we successively lodge, and if we travelled the road twice over I doubt if our experience would make us avoid them.

rochefoucauld.192.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.192.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.192.text: When our vices leave us we flatter ourselves with the idea we have left them.

rochefoucauld.193.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.193.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.193.text: There are relapses in the diseases of the mind as in those of the body; what we call a cure is often no more than an intermission or change of disease.

rochefoucauld.194.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.194.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.194.text: The defects of the mind are like the wounds of the body. Whatever care we take to heal them the scars ever remain, and there is always danger of their reopening.

rochefoucauld.195.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.195.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.195.text: The reason which often prevents us abandoning a single vice is having so many.

rochefoucauld.196.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.196.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.196.text: We easily forget those faults which are known only to ourselves.

rochefoucauld.197.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.197.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.197.text: There are men of whom we can never believe evil without having seen it. Yet there are very few in whom we should be surprised to see it.

rochefoucauld.198.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.198.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.198.text: We exaggerate the glory of some men to detract from that of others, and we should praise Prince Condé and Marshal Turenne much less if we did not want to blame them both.

rochefoucauld.199.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.199.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.199.text: The desire to appear clever often prevents our being so.

rochefoucauld.200.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.200.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.200.text: Virtue would not go far did not vanity escort her.

rochefoucauld.201.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.201.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.201.text: He who thinks he has the power to content the world greatly deceives himself, but he who thinks that the world cannot be content with him deceives himself yet more.

rochefoucauld.202.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.202.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.202.text: Falsely honest men are those who disguise their faults both to themselves and others; truly honest men are those who know them perfectly and confess them.

rochefoucauld.203.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.203.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.203.text: He is really wise who is nettled at nothing.

rochefoucauld.204.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.204.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.204.text: The coldness of women is a balance and burden they add to their beauty.

rochefoucauld.205.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.205.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.205.text: Virtue in woman is often the love of reputation and repose.

rochefoucauld.206.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.206.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.206.text: He is a truly good man who desires always to bear the inspection of good men.

rochefoucauld.207.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.207.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.207.text: Folly follows us at all stages of life. If one appears wise 'tis but because his folly is proportioned to his age and fortune.

rochefoucauld.208.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.208.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.208.text: There are foolish people who know and who skilfully use their folly.

rochefoucauld.209.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.209.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.209.text: Who lives without folly is not so wise as he thinks.

rochefoucauld.210.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.210.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.210.text: In growing old we become more foolish—and more wise.

rochefoucauld.211.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.211.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.211.text: There are people who are like farces, which are praised but for a time (however foolish and distasteful they may be).

rochefoucauld.212.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.212.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.212.text: Most people judge men only by success or by fortune.

rochefoucauld.213.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.213.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.213.text: Love of glory, fear of shame, greed of fortune, the desire to make life agreeable and comfortable, and the wish to depreciate others are often causes of that bravery so vaunted among men.

rochefoucauld.214.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.214.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.214.text: Valour in common soldiers is a perilous method of earning their living.

rochefoucauld.215.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.215.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.215.text: Perfect bravery and sheer cowardice are two extremes rarely found. The space between them is vast, and embraces all other sorts of courage. The difference between them is not less than between faces and tempers. Men will freely expose themselves at the beginning of an action, and relax and be easily discouraged if it should last. Some are content to satisfy worldly honour, and beyond that will do little else. Some are not always equally masters of their timidity. Others allow themselves to be overcome by panic; others charge because they dare not remain at their posts. Some may be found whose courage is strengthened by small perils, which prepare them to face greater dangers. Some will dare a sword cut and flinch from a bullet; others dread bullets little and fear to fight with swords. These varied kinds of courage agree in this, that night, by increasing fear and concealing gallant or cowardly actions, allows men to spare themselves. There is even a more general discretion to be observed, for we meet with no man who does all he would have done if he were assured of getting off scot-free; so that it is certain that the fear of death does somewhat subtract from valour.

rochefoucauld.216.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.216.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.216.text: Perfect valour is to do without witnesses what one would do before all the world.

rochefoucauld.217.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.217.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.217.text: Intrepidity is an extraordinary strength of soul which raises it above the troubles, disorders, and emotions which the sight of great perils can arouse in it: by this strength heroes maintain a calm aspect and preserve their reason and liberty in the most surprising and terrible accidents.

rochefoucauld.218.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.218.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.218.text: Hypocrisy is the homage vice pays to virtue.

rochefoucauld.219.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.219.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.219.text: Most men expose themselves in battle enough to save their honor, few wish to do so more than sufficiently, or than is necessary to make the design for which they expose themselves succeed.

rochefoucauld.220.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.220.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.220.text: Vanity, shame, and above all disposition, often make men brave and women chaste.

rochefoucauld.221.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.221.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.221.text: We do not wish to lose life; we do wish to gain glory, and this makes brave men show more tact and address in avoiding death, than rogues show in preserving their fortunes.

rochefoucauld.222.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.222.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.222.text: Few persons on the first approach of age do not show wherein their body, or their mind, is beginning to fail.

rochefoucauld.223.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.223.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.223.text: Gratitude is as the good faith of merchants: it holds commerce together; and we do not pay because it is just to pay debts, but because we shall thereby more easily find people who will lend.

rochefoucauld.224.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.224.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.224.text: All those who pay the debts of gratitude cannot thereby flatter themselves that they are grateful.

rochefoucauld.225.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.225.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.225.text: What makes false reckoning, as regards gratitude, is that the pride of the giver and the receiver cannot agree as to the value of the benefit.

rochefoucauld.226.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.226.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.226.text: Too great a hurry to discharge of an obligation is a kind of ingratitude.

rochefoucauld.227.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.227.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.227.text: Lucky people are bad hands at correcting their faults; they always believe that they are right when fortune backs up their vice or folly.

rochefoucauld.228.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.228.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.228.text: Pride will not owe, self-love will not pay.

rochefoucauld.229.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.229.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.229.text: The good we have received from a man should make us excuse the wrong he does us.

rochefoucauld.230.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.230.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.230.text: Nothing is so infectious as example, and we never do great good or evil without producing the like. We imitate good actions by emulation, and bad ones by the evil of our nature, which shame imprisons until example liberates.

rochefoucauld.231.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.231.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.231.text: It is great folly to wish only to be wise.

rochefoucauld.232.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.232.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.232.text: Whatever pretext we give to our afflictions it is always interest or vanity that causes them.

rochefoucauld.233.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.233.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.233.text: In afflictions there are various kinds of hypocrisy. In one, under the pretext of weeping for one dear to us we bemoan ourselves; we regret her good opinion of us, we deplore the loss of our comfort, our pleasure, our consideration. Thus the dead have the credit of tears shed for the living. I affirm 'tis a kind of hypocrisy which in these afflictions deceives itself. There is another kind not so innocent because it imposes on all the world, that is the grief of those who aspire to the glory of a noble and immortal sorrow. After Time, which absorbs all, has obliterated what sorrow they had, they still obstinately obtrude their tears, their sighs their groans, they wear a solemn face, and try to persuade others by all their acts, that their grief will end only with their life. This sad and distressing vanity is commonly found in ambitious women. As their sex closes to them all paths to glory, they strive to render themselves celebrated by showing an inconsolable affliction. There is yet another kind of tears arising from but small sources, which flow easily and cease as easily. One weeps to achieve a reputation for tenderness, weeps to be pitied, weeps to be bewept, in fact one weeps to avoid the disgrace of not weeping!

rochefoucauld.234.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.234.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.234.text: It is more often from pride than from ignorance that we are so obstinately opposed to current opinions; we find the first places taken, and we do not want to be the last.

rochefoucauld.235.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.235.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.235.text: We are easily consoled at the misfortunes of our friends when they enable us to prove our tenderness for them.

rochefoucauld.236.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.236.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.236.text: It would seem that even self-love may be the dupe of goodness and forget itself when we work for others. And yet it is but taking the shortest way to arrive at its aim, taking usury under the pretext of giving, in fact winning everybody in a subtle and delicate manner.

rochefoucauld.237.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.237.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.237.text: No one should be praised for his goodness if he has not strength enough to be wicked. All other goodness is but too often an idleness or powerlessness of will.

rochefoucauld.238.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.238.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.238.text: It is not so dangerous to do wrong to most men, as to do them too much good.

rochefoucauld.239.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.239.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.239.text: Nothing flatters our pride so much as the confidence of the great, because we regard it as the result of our worth, without remembering that generally 'tis but vanity, or the inability to keep a secret.

rochefoucauld.240.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.240.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.240.text: We may say of conformity as distinguished from beauty, that it is a symmetry which knows no rules, and a secret harmony of features both one with each other and with the colour and appearance of the person.

rochefoucauld.241.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.241.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.241.text: Flirtation is at the bottom of woman's nature, although all do not practise it, some being restrained by fear, others by sense.

rochefoucauld.242.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.242.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.242.text: We often bore others when we think we cannot possibly bore them.

rochefoucauld.243.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.243.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.243.text: Few things are impossible in themselves; application to make them succeed fails us more often than the means.

rochefoucauld.244.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.244.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.244.text: Sovereign ability consists in knowing the value of things.

rochefoucauld.245.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.245.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.245.text: There is great ability in knowing how to conceal one's ability.

rochefoucauld.246.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.246.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.246.text: What seems generosity is often disguised ambition, that despises small to run after greater interest.

rochefoucauld.247.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.247.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.247.text: The fidelity of most men is merely an invention of self-love to win confidence; a method to place us above others and to render us depositaries of the most important matters.

rochefoucauld.248.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.248.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.248.text: Magnanimity despises all, to win all.

rochefoucauld.249.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.249.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.249.text: There is no less eloquence in the voice, in the eyes and in the air of a speaker than in his choice of words.

rochefoucauld.250.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.250.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.250.text: True eloquence consists in saying all that should be, not all that could be said.

rochefoucauld.251.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.251.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.251.text: There are people whose faults become them, others whose very virtues disgrace them.

rochefoucauld.252.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.252.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.252.text: It is as common to change one's tastes, as it is uncommon to change one's inclinations.

rochefoucauld.253.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.253.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.253.text: Interest sets at work all sorts of virtues and vices.

rochefoucauld.254.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.254.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.254.text: Humility is often a feigned submission which we employ to supplant others. It is one of the devices of Pride to lower us to raise us; and truly pride transforms itself in a thousand ways, and is never so well disguised and more able to deceive than when it hides itself under the form of humility.

rochefoucauld.255.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.255.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.255.text: All feelings have their peculiar tone of voice, gestures and looks, and this harmony, as it is good or bad, pleasant or unpleasant, makes people agreeable or disagreeable.

rochefoucauld.256.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.256.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.256.text: In all professions we affect a part and an appearance to seem what we wish to be. Thus the world is merely composed of actors.

rochefoucauld.257.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.257.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.257.text: Gravity is a mysterious carriage of the body invented to conceal the want of mind.

rochefoucauld.258.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.258.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.258.text: Good taste arises more from judgment than wit.

rochefoucauld.259.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.259.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.259.text: The pleasure of love is in loving, we are happier in the passion we feel than in that we inspire.

rochefoucauld.260.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.260.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.260.text: Civility is but a desire to receive civility, and to be esteemed polite.

rochefoucauld.261.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.261.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.261.text: The usual education of young people is to inspire them with a second self-love.

rochefoucauld.262.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.262.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.262.text: There is no passion wherein self-love reigns so powerfully as in love, and one is always more ready to sacrifice the peace of the loved one than his own.

rochefoucauld.263.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.263.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.263.text: What we call liberality is often but the vanity of giving, which we like more than that we give away.

rochefoucauld.264.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.264.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.264.text: Pity is often a reflection of our own evils in the ills of others. It is a delicate foresight of the troubles into which we may fall. We help others that on like occasions we may be helped ourselves, and these services which we render, are in reality benefits we confer on ourselves by anticipation.

rochefoucauld.265.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.265.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.265.text: A narrow mind begets obstinacy, and we do not easily believe what we cannot see.

rochefoucauld.266.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.266.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.266.text: We deceive ourselves if we believe that there are violent passions like ambition and love that can triumph over others. Idleness, languishing as she is, does not often fail in being mistress; she usurps authority over all the plans and actions of life; imperceptibly consuming and destroying both passions and virtues.

rochefoucauld.267.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.267.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.267.text: A quickness in believing evil without having sufficiently examined it, is the effect of pride and laziness. We wish to find the guilty, and we do not wish to trouble ourselves in examining the crime.

rochefoucauld.268.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.268.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.268.text: We credit judges with the meanest motives, and yet we desire our reputation and fame should depend upon the judgment of men, who are all, either from their jealousy or pre-occupation or want of intelligence, opposed to us—and yet 'tis only to make these men decide in our favour that we peril in so many ways both our peace and our life.

rochefoucauld.269.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.269.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.269.text: No man is clever enough to know all the evil he does.

rochefoucauld.270.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.270.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.270.text: One honour won is a surety for more.

rochefoucauld.271.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.271.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.271.text: Youth is a continual intoxication; it is the fever of reason.

rochefoucauld.272.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.272.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.272.text: Nothing should so humiliate men who have deserved great praise, as the care they have taken to acquire it by the smallest means.

rochefoucauld.273.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.273.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.273.text: There are persons of whom the world approves who have no merit beyond the vices they use in the affairs of life.

rochefoucauld.274.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.274.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.274.text: The beauty of novelty is to love as the flower to the fruit; it lends a lustre which is easily lost, but which never returns.

rochefoucauld.275.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.275.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.275.text: Natural goodness, which boasts of being so apparent, is often smothered by the least interest.

rochefoucauld.276.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.276.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.276.text: Absence extinguishes small passions and increases great ones, as the wind will blow out a candle, and blow in a fire.

rochefoucauld.277.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.277.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.277.text: Women often think they love when they do not love. The business of a love affair, the emotion of mind that sentiment induces, the natural bias towards the pleasure of being loved, the difficulty of refusing, persuades them that they have real passion when they have but flirtation.

rochefoucauld.278.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.278.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.278.text: What makes us so often discontented with those who transact business for us is that they almost always abandon the interest of their friends for the interest of the business, because they wish to have the honour of succeeding in that which they have undertaken.

rochefoucauld.279.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.279.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.279.text: When we exaggerate the tenderness of our friends towards us, it is often less from gratitude than from a desire to exhibit our own merit.

rochefoucauld.280.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.280.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.280.text: The praise we give to new comers into the world arises from the envy we bear to those who are established.

rochefoucauld.281.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.281.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.281.text: Pride, which inspires, often serves to moderate envy.
