rochefoucauld.282.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.282.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.282.text: Some disguised lies so resemble truth, that we should judge badly were we not deceived.

rochefoucauld.283.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.283.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.283.text: Sometimes there is not less ability in knowing how to use than in giving good advice.

rochefoucauld.284.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.284.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.284.text: There are wicked people who would be much less dangerous if they were wholly without goodness.

rochefoucauld.285.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.285.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.285.text: Magnanimity is sufficiently defined by its name, nevertheless one can say it is the good sense of pride, the most noble way of receiving praise.

rochefoucauld.286.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.286.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.286.text: It is impossible to love a second time those whom we have really ceased to love.

rochefoucauld.287.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.287.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.287.text: Fertility of mind does not furnish us with so many resources on the same matter, as the lack of intelligence makes us hesitate at each thing our imagination presents, and hinders us from at first discerning which is the best.

rochefoucauld.288.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.288.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.288.text: There are matters and maladies which at certain times remedies only serve to make worse; true skill consists in knowing when it is dangerous to use them.

rochefoucauld.289.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.289.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)

rochefoucauld.290.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.290.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.290.text: There are as many errors of temper as of mind.

rochefoucauld.291.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.291.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.291.text: Man's merit, like the crops, has its season.

rochefoucauld.292.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.292.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.292.text: One may say of temper as of many buildings; it has divers aspects, some agreeable, others disagreeable.

rochefoucauld.293.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.293.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.293.text: Moderation cannot claim the merit of opposing and overcoming Ambition: they are never found together. Moderation is the languor and sloth of the soul, Ambition its activity and heat.

rochefoucauld.294.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.294.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.294.text: We always like those who admire us, we do not always like those whom we admire.

rochefoucauld.295.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.295.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.295.text: It is well that we know not all our wishes.

rochefoucauld.296.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.296.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.296.text: It is difficult to love those we do not esteem, but it is no less so to love those whom we esteem much more than ourselves.

rochefoucauld.297.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.297.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.297.text: Bodily temperaments have a common course and rule which imperceptibly affect our will. They advance in combination, and successively exercise a secret empire over us, so that, without our perceiving it, they become a great part of all our actions.

rochefoucauld.298.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.298.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.298.text: The gratitude of most men is but a secret desire of receiving greater benefits.

rochefoucauld.299.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.299.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.299.text: Almost all the world takes pleasure in paying small debts; many people show gratitude for trifling, but there is hardly one who does not show ingratitude for great favours.

rochefoucauld.300.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.300.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.300.text: There are follies as catching as infections.

rochefoucauld.301.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.301.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.301.text: Many people despise, but few know how to bestow wealth.

rochefoucauld.302.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.302.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.302.text: Only in things of small value we usually are bold enough not to trust to appearances.

rochefoucauld.303.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.303.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.303.text: Whatever good quality may be imputed to us, we ourselves find nothing new in it.

rochefoucauld.304.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.304.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.304.text: We may forgive those who bore us, we cannot forgive those whom we bore.

rochefoucauld.305.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.305.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.305.text: Interest which is accused of all our misdeeds often should be praised for our good deeds.

rochefoucauld.306.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.306.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.306.text: We find very few ungrateful people when we are able to confer favours.

rochefoucauld.307.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.307.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.307.text: It is as proper to be boastful alone as it is ridiculous to be so in company.

rochefoucauld.308.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.308.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.308.text: Moderation is made a virtue to limit the ambition of the great; to console ordinary people for their small fortune and equally small ability.

rochefoucauld.309.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.309.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.309.text: There are persons fated to be fools, who commit follies not only by choice, but who are forced by fortune to do so.

rochefoucauld.310.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.310.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.310.text: Sometimes there are accidents in our life the skilful extrication from which demands a little folly.

rochefoucauld.311.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.311.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.311.text: If there be men whose folly has never appeared, it is because it has never been closely looked for.

rochefoucauld.312.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.312.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.312.text: Lovers are never tired of each other,—they always speak of themselves.

rochefoucauld.313.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.313.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.313.text: How is it that our memory is good enough to retain the least triviality that happens to us, and yet not good enough to recollect how often we have told it to the same person?

rochefoucauld.314.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.314.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.314.text: The extreme delight we take in talking of ourselves should warn us that it is not shared by those who listen.

rochefoucauld.315.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.315.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.315.text: What commonly hinders us from showing the recesses of our heart to our friends, is not the distrust we have of them, but that we have of ourselves.

rochefoucauld.316.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.316.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)

rochefoucauld.317.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.317.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.317.text: 'Tis a small misfortune to oblige an ungrateful man; but it is unbearable to be obliged by a scoundrel.

rochefoucauld.318.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.318.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.318.text: We may find means to cure a fool of his folly, but there are none to set straight a cross-grained spirit.

rochefoucauld.319.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.319.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.319.text: If we take the liberty to dwell on their faults we cannot long preserve the feelings we should hold towards our friends and benefactors.

rochefoucauld.320.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.320.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.320.text: To praise princes for virtues they do not possess is but to reproach them with impunity.

rochefoucauld.321.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.321.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.321.text: We are nearer loving those who hate us, than those who love us more than we desire.

rochefoucauld.322.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.322.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.322.text: Those only are despicable who fear to be despised.

rochefoucauld.323.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.323.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.323.text: Our wisdom is no less at the mercy of Fortune than our goods.

rochefoucauld.324.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.324.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.324.text: There is more self-love than love in jealousy.

rochefoucauld.325.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.325.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.325.text: We often comfort ourselves by the weakness of evils, for which reason has not the strength to console us.

rochefoucauld.326.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.326.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.326.text: Ridicule dishonours more than dishonour itself.

rochefoucauld.327.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.327.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.327.text: We own to small faults to persuade others that we have not great ones.

rochefoucauld.328.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.328.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.328.text: Envy is more irreconcilable than hatred.

rochefoucauld.329.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.329.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.329.text: We believe, sometimes, that we hate flattery —we only dislike the method.

rochefoucauld.330.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.330.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.330.text: We pardon in the degree that we love.

rochefoucauld.331.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.331.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.331.text: It is more difficult to be faithful to a mistress when one is happy, than when we are ill-treated by her.

rochefoucauld.332.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.332.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.332.text: Women do not know all their powers of flirtation.

rochefoucauld.333.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.333.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.333.text: Women cannot be completely severe unless they hate.

rochefoucauld.334.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.334.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.334.text: Women can less easily resign flirtations than love.

rochefoucauld.335.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.335.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.335.text: In love deceit almost always goes further than mistrust.

rochefoucauld.336.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.336.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.336.text: There is a kind of love, the excess of which forbids jealousy.

rochefoucauld.337.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.337.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.337.text: There are certain good qualities as there are senses, and those who want them can neither perceive nor understand them.

rochefoucauld.338.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.338.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.338.text: When our hatred is too bitter it places us below those whom we hate.

rochefoucauld.339.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.339.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.339.text: We only appreciate our good or evil in proportion to our self-love.

rochefoucauld.340.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.340.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.340.text: The wit of most women rather strengthens their folly than their reason.

rochefoucauld.341.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.341.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.341.text: The heat of youth is not more opposed to safety than the coldness of age.

rochefoucauld.342.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.342.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.342.text: The accent of our native country dwells in the heart and mind as well as on the tongue.

rochefoucauld.343.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.343.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.343.text: To be a great man one should know how to profit by every phase of fortune.

rochefoucauld.344.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.344.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.344.text: Most men, like plants, possess hidden qualities which chance discovers.

rochefoucauld.345.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.345.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.345.text: Opportunity makes us known to others, but more to ourselves.

rochefoucauld.346.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.346.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.346.text: If a woman's temper is beyond control there can be no control of the mind or heart.

rochefoucauld.347.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.347.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.347.text: We hardly find any persons of good sense, save those who agree with us.

rochefoucauld.348.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.348.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.348.text: When one loves one doubts even what one most believes.

rochefoucauld.349.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.349.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.349.text: The greatest miracle of love is to eradicate flirtation.

rochefoucauld.350.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.350.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.350.text: Why we hate with so much bitterness those who deceive us is because they think themselves more clever than we are.

rochefoucauld.351.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.351.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.351.text: We have much trouble to break with one, when we no longer are in love.

rochefoucauld.352.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.352.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.352.text: We almost always are bored with persons with whom we should not be bored.

rochefoucauld.353.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.353.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.353.text: A gentleman may love like a lunatic, but not like a beast.

rochefoucauld.354.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.354.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.354.text: There are certain defects which well mounted glitter like virtue itself.

rochefoucauld.355.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.355.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.355.text: Sometimes we lose friends for whose loss our regret is greater than our grief, and others for whom our grief is greater than our regret.

rochefoucauld.356.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.356.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.356.text: Usually we only praise heartily those who admire us.

rochefoucauld.357.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.357.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.357.text: Little minds are too much wounded by little things; great minds see all and are not even hurt.

rochefoucauld.358.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.358.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.358.text: Humility is the true proof of Christian virtues; without it we retain all our faults, and they are only covered by pride to hide them from others, and often from ourselves.

rochefoucauld.359.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.359.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.359.text: Infidelities should extinguish love, and we ought not to be jealous when we have cause to be so. No persons escape causing jealousy who are worthy of exciting it.

rochefoucauld.360.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.360.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.360.text: We are more humiliated by the least infidelity towards us, than by our greatest towards others.

rochefoucauld.361.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.361.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.361.text: Jealousy is always born with love, but does not always die with it.

rochefoucauld.362.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.362.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.362.text: Most women do not grieve so much for the death of their lovers for love's-sake, as to show they were worthy of being beloved.

rochefoucauld.363.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.363.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.363.text: The evils we do to others give us less pain than those we do to ourselves.

rochefoucauld.364.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.364.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.364.text: We well know that it is bad taste to talk of our wives; but we do not so well know that it is the same to speak of ourselves.

rochefoucauld.365.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.365.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.365.text: There are virtues which degenerate into vices when they arise from Nature, and others which when acquired are never perfect. For example, reason must teach us to manage our estate and our confidence, while Nature should have given us goodness and valour.

rochefoucauld.366.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.366.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.366.text: However we distrust the sincerity of those whom we talk with, we always believe them more sincere with us than with others.

rochefoucauld.367.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.367.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.367.text: There are few virtuous women who are not tired of their part.

rochefoucauld.368.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.368.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.368.text: The greater number of good women are like concealed treasures, safe as no one has searched for them.

rochefoucauld.369.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.369.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.369.text: The violences we put upon ourselves to escape love are often more cruel than the cruelty of those we love.

rochefoucauld.370.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.370.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.370.text: There are not many cowards who know the whole of their fear.

rochefoucauld.371.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.371.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.371.text: It is generally the fault of the loved one not to perceive when love ceases.

rochefoucauld.372.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.372.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.372.text: Most young people think they are natural when they are only boorish and rude.

rochefoucauld.373.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.373.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.373.text: Some tears after having deceived others deceive ourselves.

rochefoucauld.374.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.374.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.374.text: If we think we love a woman for love of herself we are greatly deceived.

rochefoucauld.375.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.375.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.375.text: Ordinary men commonly condemn what is beyond them.

rochefoucauld.376.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.376.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.376.text: Envy is destroyed by true friendship, flirtation by true love.

rochefoucauld.377.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.377.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.377.text: The greatest mistake of penetration is not to have fallen short, but to have gone too far.

rochefoucauld.378.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.378.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.378.text: We may bestow advice, but we cannot inspire the conduct.

rochefoucauld.379.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.379.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.379.text: As our merit declines so also does our taste.

rochefoucauld.380.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.380.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.380.text: Fortune makes visible our virtues or our vices, as light does objects.

rochefoucauld.381.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.381.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.381.text: The struggle we undergo to remain faithful to one we love is little better than infidelity.

rochefoucauld.382.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.382.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.382.text: Our actions are like the rhymed ends of blank verses (Bouts-Rimés) where to each one puts what construction he pleases.

rochefoucauld.383.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.383.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.383.text: The desire of talking about ourselves, and of putting our faults in the light we wish them to be seen, forms a great part of our sincerity.

rochefoucauld.384.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.384.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.384.text: We should only be astonished at still being able to be astonished.

rochefoucauld.385.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.385.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.385.text: It is equally as difficult to be contented when one has too much or too little love.

rochefoucauld.386.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.386.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.386.text: No people are more often wrong than those who will not allow themselves to be wrong.

rochefoucauld.387.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.387.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.387.text: A fool has not stuff in him to be good.

rochefoucauld.388.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.388.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.388.text: If vanity does not overthrow all virtues, at least she makes them totter.

rochefoucauld.389.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.389.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.389.text: What makes the vanity of others unsupportable is that it wounds our own.

rochefoucauld.390.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.390.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.390.text: We give up more easily our interest than our taste.

rochefoucauld.391.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.391.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.391.text: Fortune appears so blind to none as to those to whom she has done no good.

rochefoucauld.392.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.392.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.392.text: We should manage fortune like our health, enjoy it when it is good, be patient when it is bad, and never resort to strong remedies but in an extremity.

rochefoucauld.393.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.393.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.393.text: Awkwardness sometimes disappears in the camp, never in the court.

rochefoucauld.394.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.394.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.394.text: A man is often more clever than one other, but not than all others.

rochefoucauld.395.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.395.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.395.text: We are often less unhappy at being deceived by one we loved, than on being deceived.

rochefoucauld.396.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.396.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.396.text: We keep our first lover for a long time—if we do not get a second.

rochefoucauld.397.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.397.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.397.text: We have not the courage to say generally that we have no faults, and that our enemies have no good qualities; but in fact we are not far from believing so.

rochefoucauld.398.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.398.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.398.text: Of all our faults that which we most readily admit is idleness: we believe that it makes all virtues ineffectual, and that without utterly destroying, it at least suspends their operation.

rochefoucauld.399.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.399.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.399.text: There is a kind of greatness which does not depend upon fortune: it is a certain manner what distinguishes us, and which seems to destine us for great things; it is the value we insensibly set upon ourselves; it is by this quality that we gain the deference of other men, and it is this which commonly raises us more above them, than birth, rank, or even merit itself.

rochefoucauld.400.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.400.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.400.text: There may be talent without position, but there is no position without some kind of talent.

rochefoucauld.401.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.401.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.401.text: Rank is to merit what dress is to a pretty woman.

rochefoucauld.402.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.402.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.402.text: What we find the least of in flirtation is love.

rochefoucauld.403.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.403.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.403.text: Fortune sometimes uses our faults to exalt us, and there are tiresome people whose deserts would be ill rewarded if we did not desire to purchase their absence.

rochefoucauld.404.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.404.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.404.text: It appears that nature has hid at the bottom of our hearts talents and abilities unknown to us. It is only the passions that have the power of bringing them to light, and sometimes give us views more true and more perfect than art could possibly do.

rochefoucauld.405.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.405.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.405.text: We reach quite inexperienced the different stages of life, and often, in spite of the number of our years, we lack experience.

rochefoucauld.406.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.406.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.406.text: Flirts make it a point of honour to be jealous of their lovers, to conceal their envy of other women.

rochefoucauld.407.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.407.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.407.text: It may well be that those who have trapped us by their tricks do not seem to us so foolish as we seem to ourselves when trapped by the tricks of others.

rochefoucauld.408.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.408.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.408.text: The most dangerous folly of old persons who have been loveable is to forget that they are no longer so.

rochefoucauld.409.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.409.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.409.text: We should often be ashamed of our very best actions if the world only saw the motives which caused them.

rochefoucauld.410.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.410.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.410.text: The greatest effort of friendship is not to show our faults to a friend, but to show him his own.

rochefoucauld.411.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.411.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.411.text: Whatever disgrace we may have deserved, it is almost always in our power to re-establish our character.

rochefoucauld.412.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.412.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.412.text: A man cannot please long who has only one kind of wit.

rochefoucauld.413.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.413.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.413.text: Idiots and lunatics see only their own wit.

rochefoucauld.414.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.414.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.414.text: Wit sometimes enables us to act rudely with impunity.

rochefoucauld.415.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.415.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.415.text: The vivacity which increases in old age is not far removed from folly.

rochefoucauld.416.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.416.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.416.text: In love the quickest is always the best cure.

rochefoucauld.417.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.417.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.417.text: Young women who do not want to appear flirts, and old men who do not want to appear ridiculous, should not talk of love as a matter wherein they can have any interest.

rochefoucauld.418.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.418.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.418.text: We may seem great in a post beneath our capacity, but we oftener seem little in a post above it.

rochefoucauld.419.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.419.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.419.text: We often believe we have constancy in misfortune when we have nothing but debasement, and we suffer misfortunes without regarding them as cowards who let themselves be killed from fear of defending themselves.

rochefoucauld.420.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.420.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.420.text: Conceit causes more conversation than wit.

rochefoucauld.421.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.421.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.421.text: All passions make us commit some faults, love alone makes us ridiculous.

rochefoucauld.422.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.422.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.422.text: Few know how to be old.

rochefoucauld.423.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.423.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.423.text: We often credit ourselves with vices the reverse of what we have, thus when weak we boast of our obstinacy.

rochefoucauld.424.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.424.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.424.text: Penetration has a spice of divination in it which tickles our vanity more than any other quality of the mind.

rochefoucauld.425.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.425.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.425.text: The charm of novelty and old custom, however opposite to each other, equally blind us to the faults of our friends.

rochefoucauld.426.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.426.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.426.text: Most friends sicken us of friendship, most devotees of devotion.

rochefoucauld.427.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.427.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.427.text: We easily forgive in our friends those faults we do not perceive.

rochefoucauld.428.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.428.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.428.text: Women who love, pardon more readily great indiscretions than little infidelities.

rochefoucauld.429.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.429.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.429.text: In the old age of love as in life we still survive for the evils, though no longer for the pleasures.

rochefoucauld.430.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.430.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.430.text: Nothing prevents our being unaffected so much as our desire to seem so.

rochefoucauld.431.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.431.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.431.text: To praise good actions heartily is in some measure to take part in them.

rochefoucauld.432.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.432.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.432.text: The most certain sign of being born with great qualities is to be born without envy.

rochefoucauld.433.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.433.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.433.text: When our friends have deceived us we owe them but indifference to the tokens of their friendship, yet for their misfortunes we always owe them pity.

rochefoucauld.434.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.434.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.434.text: Luck and temper rule the world.

rochefoucauld.435.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.435.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.435.text: It is far easier to know men than to know man.

rochefoucauld.436.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.436.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.436.text: We should not judge of a man's merit by his great abilities, but by the use he makes of them.

rochefoucauld.437.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.437.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.437.text: There is a certain lively gratitude which not only releases us from benefits received, but which also, by making a return to our friends as payment, renders them indebted to us.

rochefoucauld.438.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.438.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.438.text: We should earnestly desire but few things if we clearly knew what we desired.

rochefoucauld.439.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.439.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.439.text: The cause why the majority of women are so little given to friendship is, that it is insipid after having felt love.

rochefoucauld.440.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.440.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.440.text: As in friendship so in love, we are often happier from ignorance than from knowledge.

rochefoucauld.441.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.441.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.441.text: We try to make a virtue of vices we are loth to correct.

rochefoucauld.442.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.442.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.442.text: The most violent passions give some respite, but vanity always disturbs us.

rochefoucauld.443.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.443.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.443.text: Old fools are more foolish than young fools.

rochefoucauld.444.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.444.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.444.text: Weakness is more hostile to virtue than vice.

rochefoucauld.445.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.445.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.445.text: What makes the grief of shame and jealousy so acute is that vanity cannot aid us in enduring them.

rochefoucauld.446.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.446.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.446.text: Propriety is the least of all laws, but the most obeyed.

rochefoucauld.447.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.447.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.447.text: A well-trained mind has less difficulty in submitting to than in guiding an ill-trained mind.

rochefoucauld.448.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.448.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.448.text: When fortune surprises us by giving us some great office without having gradually led us to expect it, or without having raised our hopes, it is well nigh impossible to occupy it well, and to appear worthy to fill it.

rochefoucauld.449.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.449.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.449.text: Our pride is often increased by what we retrench from our other faults.

rochefoucauld.450.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.450.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.450.text: No fools so wearisome as those who have some wit.

rochefoucauld.451.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.451.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.451.text: No one believes that in every respect he is behind the man he considers the ablest in the world.

rochefoucauld.452.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.452.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.452.text: In great matters we should not try so much to create opportunities as to utilise those that offer themselves.

rochefoucauld.453.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.453.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.453.text: There are few occasions when we should make a bad bargain by giving up the good on condition that no ill was said of us.

rochefoucauld.454.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.454.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.454.text: However disposed the world may be to judge wrongly, it far oftener favours false merit than does justice to true.

rochefoucauld.455.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.455.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.455.text: Sometimes we meet a fool with wit, never one with discretion.

rochefoucauld.456.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.456.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.456.text: We should gain more by letting the world see what we are than by trying to seem what we are not.

rochefoucauld.457.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.457.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.457.text: Our enemies come nearer the truth in the opinions they form of us than we do in our opinion of ourselves.

rochefoucauld.458.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.458.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.458.text: There are many remedies to cure love, yet none are infallible.

rochefoucauld.459.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.459.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.459.text: It would be well for us if we knew all our passions make us do.

rochefoucauld.460.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.460.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.460.text: Age is a tyrant who forbids at the penalty of life all the pleasures of youth.

rochefoucauld.461.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.461.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.461.text: The same pride which makes us blame faults from which we believe ourselves free causes us to despise the good qualities we have not.

rochefoucauld.462.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.462.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.462.text: There is often more pride than goodness in our grief for our enemies' miseries; it is to show how superior we are to them, that we bestow on them the sign of our compassion.

rochefoucauld.463.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.463.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.463.text: There exists an excess of good and evil which surpasses our comprehension.

rochefoucauld.464.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.464.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.464.text: Innocence is most fortunate if it finds the same protection as crime.

rochefoucauld.465.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.465.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.465.text: Of all the violent passions the one that becomes a woman best is love.

rochefoucauld.466.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.466.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.466.text: Vanity makes us sin more against our taste than reason.

rochefoucauld.467.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.467.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.467.text: Some bad qualities form great talents.

rochefoucauld.468.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.468.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.468.text: We never desire earnestly what we desire in reason.

rochefoucauld.469.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.469.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.469.text: All our qualities are uncertain and doubtful, both the good as well as the bad, and nearly all are creatures of opportunities.

rochefoucauld.470.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.470.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.470.text: In their first passion women love their lovers, in all the others they love love.

rochefoucauld.471.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.471.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.471.text: Pride as the other passions has its follies. We are ashamed to own we are jealous, and yet we plume ourselves in having been and being able to be so.

rochefoucauld.472.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.472.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.472.text: However rare true love is, true friendship is rarer.

rochefoucauld.473.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.473.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.473.text: There are few women whose charm survives their beauty.

rochefoucauld.474.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.474.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.474.text: The desire to be pitied or to be admired often forms the greater part of our confidence.

rochefoucauld.475.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.475.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.475.text: Our envy always lasts longer than the happiness of those we envy.

rochefoucauld.476.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.476.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.476.text: The same firmness that enables us to resist love enables us to make our resistance durable and lasting. So weak persons who are always excited by passions are seldom really possessed of any.

rochefoucauld.477.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.477.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.477.text: Fancy does not enable us to invent so many different contradictions as there are by nature in every heart.

rochefoucauld.478.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.478.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.478.text: It is only people who possess firmness who can possess true gentleness. In those who appear gentle it is generally only weakness, which is readily converted into harshness.

rochefoucauld.479.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.479.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.479.text: Timidity is a fault which is dangerous to blame in those we desire to cure of it.

rochefoucauld.480.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.480.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.480.text: Nothing is rarer than true good nature, those who think they have it are generally only pliant or weak.

rochefoucauld.481.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.481.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.481.text: The mind attaches itself by idleness and habit to whatever is easy or pleasant. This habit always places bounds to our knowledge, and no one has ever yet taken the pains to enlarge and expand his mind to the full extent of its capacities.

rochefoucauld.482.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.482.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.482.text: Usually we are more satirical from vanity than malice.

rochefoucauld.483.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.483.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.483.text: When the heart is still disturbed by the relics of a passion it is proner to take up a new one than when wholly cured.

rochefoucauld.484.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.484.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.484.text: Those who have had great passions often find all their lives made miserable in being cured of them.

rochefoucauld.485.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.485.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.485.text: More persons exist without self-love than without envy.

rochefoucauld.486.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.486.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.486.text: We have more idleness in the mind than in the body.

rochefoucauld.487.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.487.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.487.text: The calm or disturbance of our mind does not depend so much on what we regard as the more important things of life, as in a judicious or injudicious arrangement of the little things of daily occurrence.

rochefoucauld.488.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.488.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.488.text: However wicked men may be, they do not dare openly to appear the enemies of virtue, and when they desire to persecute her they either pretend to believe her false or attribute crimes to her.

rochefoucauld.489.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.489.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.489.text: We often go from love to ambition, but we never return from ambition to love.

rochefoucauld.490.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.490.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.490.text: Extreme avarice is nearly always mistaken, there is no passion which is oftener further away from its mark, nor upon which the present has so much power to the prejudice of the future.

rochefoucauld.491.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.491.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.491.text: Avarice often produces opposite results: there are an infinite number of persons who sacrifice their property to doubtful and distant expectations, others mistake great future advantages for small present interests.

rochefoucauld.492.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.492.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.492.text: It appears that men do not find they have enough faults, as they increase the number by certain peculiar qualities that they affect to assume, and which they cultivate with so great assiduity that at length they become natural faults, which they can no longer correct.

rochefoucauld.493.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.493.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.493.text: What makes us see that men know their faults better than we imagine, is that they are never wrong when they speak of their conduct; the same self-love that usually blinds them enlightens them, and gives them such true views as to make them suppress or disguise the smallest thing that might be censured.

rochefoucauld.494.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.494.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.494.text: Young men entering life should be either shy or bold; a solemn and sedate manner usually degenerates into impertinence.

rochefoucauld.495.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.495.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.495.text: Quarrels would not last long if the fault was only on one side.

rochefoucauld.496.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.496.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.496.text: It is valueless to a woman to be young unless pretty, or to be pretty unless young.

rochefoucauld.497.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.497.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.497.text: Some persons are so frivolous and fickle that they are as far removed from real defects as from substantial qualities.

rochefoucauld.498.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.498.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.498.text: We do not usually reckon a woman's first flirtation until she has had a second.

rochefoucauld.499.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.499.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.499.text: Some people are so self-occupied that when in love they find a mode by which to be engrossed with the passion without being so with the person they love.

rochefoucauld.500.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.500.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.500.text: Love, though so very agreeable, pleases more by its ways than by itself.

rochefoucauld.501.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.501.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.501.text: A little wit with good sense bores less in the long run than much wit with ill nature.

rochefoucauld.502.author: François de La Rochefoucauld
rochefoucauld.502.translator: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)
rochefoucauld.502.text: Jealousy is the worst of all evils, yet the one that is least pitied by those who cause it.
